notes: One set issued in two waves, 660 base card numbers.

provenance.notes: This document prints the statistic a League Leaders card ranks, which no other year here does: "48 Guerrero Jr./Perez/Ohtani AL HR Leaders League Leaders" carries LL and HRL together, twelve cards across six statistics. It also prints AL, NL and MLB where the team goes on those cards, and RC where other years print Rookie.

Diamond Greats Die Cuts is one 50-card insert, DGDC-1 to DGDC-50, because the two series number it 1-25 and 26-50 and merge without collision. Its autographs do not follow suit. The Series 1 list runs DGDC-1 to DGDC-9 and names the same players the insert does on 16 of its 17 rows, the seventeenth differing only in that Topps prints Montreal Expos unaccented there and Montréal Expos in the insert, so it is recorded as varying the insert. The Series 2 list also runs DGDC-1 to DGDC-9 and names a different player on every one of its 10 rows — DGDC-1 is Nolan Ryan where the insert has Mike Trout. It is numbered independently of the insert, so it declares no varies; saying otherwise would pass validation, which checks that numbers exist and cannot check that they mean the same card. The two lists are kept per series for the same reason. Stars of MLB Chrome Variation is headed a variation by Topps but numbers itself SMLBC-1 to SMLBC-30 against the insert's SMLB-1 to SMLB-30, so it introduces thirty cards and is an insert.

provenance.covers: the Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 Gimmicks variations
provenance.notes: 149 cards no Topps checklist lists, in two waves of 71 and 78. That source gives numbers and names only, so every team here is this set's own. Where the gimmick shows the base card's player, 116 of the 149, the team is that card's. Where it shows somebody else, almost always a legend, the team is still the base card's: Derek Jeter sits on Gio Urshela's Yankees #23, Roberto Clemente on Ben Gamel's Pirates #285, and 29 of the 30 legends checked this way are a legend of the franchise whose card they replace. The single exception is #42, where Jackie Robinson replaces Mitch Moreland of the Oakland Athletics: 42 is retired across the league, so that card is a jersey-number gimmick rather than a franchise one, and its team is the Brooklyn Dodgers, the only team this set prints for Robinson. Names follow this set where it prints the player and that source otherwise, which is why #103 reads MIke Yastrzemksi with Topps' two typos intact. Two numbers carry two gimmicks each, #103 with Yastrzemksi and Willie Mays and #660 with Bobby Witt Jr. and Shohei Ohtani, which the row key separates by name. Production codes ending 560 in Series 1 and 865 in Series 2, and an estimated 3,000 copies of each, are recorded nowhere else: the codes have no column and the figure is an estimate, which this repo does not keep. Tiers 2 and 3 follow, 48 cards and 10, on the same team rule with one addition. Four Tier 2 legends are not legends of the franchise whose card they replace, and all four are jersey-number gimmicks: #42 and #442 are Jackie Robinson, whose 42 is retired across the league, and #4 and #444 are Lou Gehrig, who wore 4. On those the number is the subject, so the team is the player's — Brooklyn Dodgers from this set, New York Yankees from the 23 rows that print Gehrig elsewhere in this repo, Topps' own form in both cases. Every other Tier 2 legend matches its base card's franchise, which is why #49 Babe Ruth and #51 Nolan Ryan are left on the base team rather than treated as jersey numbers. Tier 3 settles what the wave headings mean: its Series One group is five Atlanta Braves photographed after the 2021 World Series, and two of them are #401 and #507, Series 2 numbers. Its Series Two group is five mascot heads on #215 to #315, all Series 1 numbers. So the heading names the packs a gimmick came in, not the numbering it varies, and the two are independent — which is also the answer to the same contradiction recorded against 2024's Kevin Hart Gimmicks. UNRESOLVED: the mascot on #300 is the Swingin' Friar, San Diego's, on a card this set prints as Vladimir Guerrero Jr. of the Toronto Blue Jays, where the other four mascots each match their card's team. That source says a player's face is replaced with their own team's mascot, so either its number or its mascot is wrong; the row keeps the card's team and the conflict is recorded rather than resolved. Each tier is one checklist rather than one per wave. For Tiers 1 and 2 that loses nothing, because their waves split exactly on the numbering — every Series 1 gimmick is numbered 1 to 330 and every Series 2 one 331 to 660 — so which packs a card came in, and therefore its production code, stays readable from its number against series[]. Tier 3 is the reason the merge needed thinking about: its waves cross the numbering, five Braves including #401 and #507 in Series 1 packs and five mascots on #215 to #315 in Series 2 packs, so the number cannot say which. Its rows carry the group in variation_note, World Series Celebration or Mascot Head, which recovers the wave and the production code and also names the two gimmicks, which the wave alone never did. The production code is on the rows, not only in this note, because it is the one printed thing separating tiers on a card that appears in more than one — #103 Willie Mays is a Tier 1 gimmick coded 560 and a Tier 2 gimmick coded 561, and nothing else on the two cards distinguishes them. Codes are 560 and 865 for Tier 1, 561 and 866 for Tier 2, 562 and 867 for Tier 3, the first of each pair being the Series 1 packs. Three teams were wrong when these were first written and are corrected here: #658 Spencer Torkelson, #659 Julio Rodriguez and #660 Bobby Witt Jr. had been given the teams of the base cards they replace — Justin Bruihl's Dodgers, LaMonte Wade Jr.'s Giants and Shohei Ohtani's Angels. The rule that a gimmick keeps its base card's team holds for legends, who are chosen as legends of that franchise, and fails for rookies, who are simply the year's rookies. Their teams are the ones this repo prints for them elsewhere: Detroit, Seattle and Kansas City. The check that found them ignores these three files, since rows cannot be their own evidence.

provenance.source: Baseball Card Pedia, 2022 Topps — factory sets
provenance.covers: the three factory set checklists and the Chrome Refractor parallels
provenance.notes: Factory Set Rookie Variations is five cards in every retail factory set, on base numbers with the base players, each incorrectly marked CHROME on the reverse below the card number — Topps' own error, recorded on the rows. Factory Set Rookie Bonus is three cards marked COMPLETE SETS, replacing Justin Bruihl, LaMonte Wade Jr. and Shohei Ohtani on #658 to #660 with Spencer Torkelson, Julio Rodriguez and Bobby Witt Jr. Factory Set All-Stars is an insert rather than a variation: its numbers are 1 to 5 and this set's #1 to #5 are Shohei Ohtani, Craig Kimbrel, Huascar Ynoa, Travis d'Arnaud and Rougned Odor, so it introduces five cards and declares no varies. Its teams come from Trading Card Database, except that Ohtani is recorded as Angels, the form Topps prints throughout this set, where that database renders Los Angeles Angels. It carries the same CHROME misprint. The Chrome Refractor Rookie Variation is a parallel, not a checklist: that source says its list is identical to the five Rookie Variations and that the same photography is used, which is a finish change over the same photo. It came in Green Box factory sets at Target, and its own four parallels are Gold Refractor /50, Orange /25, Red /5 and SuperFractor one-of-one. Not recorded: the Chrome Rookie Relic and Autographed Relic Refractors of the Teal Box sets. They are the same five players but numbered CRR-XX and CRAR-XX by initials, and that source gives the rule and one example, CRR-WF, rather than the five numbers. Initials are not derivable — 2023 Topps numbers the same kind of card JROD, MMA and ABR — so inventing four of them would be a guess. The estimate of 6,322 copies of each base Refractor is an estimate and is not recorded either.

provenance.source: Baseball Card Pedia, 2022 Topps — base parallels
provenance.covers: which parallels cover every base card
provenance.notes: "All 660 base cards are available in the following parallels", followed by 18 entries, recorded here as coverage full. Printing Plates is one entry there, a set of four for each card, and is declared as four because a plate is a distinct one-of-one a collector owns and one entry cannot record owning the cyan one — the same reading applied to 2024, 2025 and 2026. The page was read twice with differently worded requests and gave identical names and figures both times, which is the check that matters here: a summarising fetch has misread a print-run column in this repo before. 2022's ladder is foils and foilboards rather than the foilboard-only run of 2024, and its Gold is /2022 on the year convention Topps keeps in every year here. Four parallels are recorded with distributions that narrow where they were sold rather than what they cover: Gold Foil in Jumbo packs, Royal Blue at retail, Purple in packs sold at Meijer stores, Black in Hobby and Jumbo. Striped Foilboard and Shimmer Foilboard are the packs of five in the Walmart and Hobby factory sets. NOT declared: the four Walmart factory set parallels of that section, Gold Star, Blue Star, Orange Star and FoilFractor. Their limits are given as sets — 299 sets, 99 sets, one set as a redemption — which is a statement about how many sets exist rather than a number printed on a card, and print_run records only what a card carries.

provenance.source: Trading Card Database, 2022 Topps Baseball Errors/Variations (PDF export)
provenance.notes:
Forty-nine cards, every one a Series 1 number carrying RC, listed by that database as "Factory set, Large RC logo". Each was checked against base.csv on name before being written, since the list was transcribed from a printed export rather than parsed; all 49 matched. The file began as a single row for #12 Gavin Sheets, which is how the programme came to light — a card attested by that database and documented nowhere on Baseball Card Pedia's 2022 page.

That database lists a second group of 40, all Series 2 numbers, described as "Factory set, white outline around RC logo". They are not recorded here. Same idea, different treatment and different wave, and nothing yet says whether Topps meant them as one programme of 89 or two of 49 and 40.

UNRESOLVED, and it matters more: #187 Jarren Duran, #215 Wander Franco and #243 Brandon Marsh are now in this file and in Factory Set Rookie Variations, which holds the five that page calls "a set of five Rookie Variations included in each retail factory set". Its other two, #421 Shane Baz and #537 Oneil Cruz, are in the white-outline group. So all five of that page's Rookie Variations are factory-set RC logo variations in this database's reading, split by series exactly as the two treatments split, which makes the five look like a partial list of the 89 rather than a programme of their own. If that is right, this repo currently counts those three cards twice and the five-card checklist should be retired into these. The one thing arguing against it is that the page says those five are incorrectly marked CHROME on the reverse, which this database does not mention for any of the 89. Both records are kept as their sources state them until a card settles it.
